cards.title: 5.1 Similar Polygons and the Definition of Similarity
body: 5.1 Similar Polygons and the Definition of Similarity

**Definition:** Two polygons are **Similar Polygons** if and only if there is a one-to-one correspondence between their vertices such that all corresponding angles are congruent (equal in measure) and all corresponding sides are proportional (their ratios are equal).

### Deep Dive
Geometric similarity is a fundamental concept in Euclidean geometry that describes shapes with the identical form but different sizes. While congruence requires shapes to be completely identical in both shape and size, similarity focuses strictly on shape. This relationship can be visualized as scaling a figure up or down without distorting its proportions. To preserve the geometric structure of a polygon during scaling, two conditions must be met: all corresponding angles must remain unchanged, and all corresponding sides must scale by the exact same

cards.title: Similarity and the Geometry of Shape
body: In practical applications, similarity is the mathematical foundation for technical drawing, cartography, and scale modeling. Blueprints and maps are highly precise, scaled-down representations of real buildings and geographic regions. Cartographers use a constant scale factor to ensure that distances measured on a map can be converted accurately into real-world distances, preserving spatial relationships.

In digital graphics and computer-aided design (CAD), similarity is used whenever an image or vector graphic is resized. Resizing an image while maintaining its aspect ratio is a real-time application of geometric similarity. If the horizontal and vertical dimensions are not scaled by the same ratio, the image becomes distorted, showing how preserving proportional ratios is essential for maintaining visual integrity.

cards.title: Similarity and the Geometry of Shape
body:
The **Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales' Theorem)** is a fundamental tool for proving and applying similarity. If we have a triangle $$\Delta ABC$$ and draw a line $$DE$$ parallel to the base $$BC$$ (such that $$D$$ lies on $$AB$$ and $$E$$ lies on $$AC$$), the theorem states that:
$$\frac{AD}{DB} = \frac{AE}{EC}$$
Adding $$1$$ to both sides of this equation yields another useful form of the proportion: $$\frac{AB}{AD} = \frac{AC}{AE}$$, which shows that the smaller triangle $$\Delta ADE$$ is similar to the larger triangle $$\Delta ABC$$.

The converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem is also true: if a line divides any two sides of a triangle in the exact same ratio, then the line must be parallel to the third side. This biconditional relationship allows geometricians to prove that lines are parallel within complex structures simply by measuring segment lengths.

This uniform scaling ratio is known as the **scale factor** (or constant of proportionality, denoted by $$k$$). If we have two similar quadrilaterals, $$ABCD$$ and $$PQRS$$, we write their relationship as $$ABCD \sim PQRS$$. This notation implies that the angle measures match exactly ($$\angle A \cong \angle P$$, $$\angle B \cong \angle Q$$, etc.) and that the ratios of their corresponding side lengths are equal:
$$\frac{AB}{PQ} = \frac{BC}{QR} = \frac{CD}{RS} = \frac{DA}{SP} = k$$
If the scale factor $$k = 1$$, the polygons are both similar and congruent, showing that congruence is a special case of similarity.

cards.title: Similarity and the Geometry of Shape
body: To analyze similar polygons algebraically, we can set up proportions using their corresponding side lengths. If we are given two similar shapes and know some of their side lengths, we can write a rational equation to solve for the unknown dimensions. This algebraic approach is a powerful tool for calculating distances that are difficult or impossible to measure directly.

| Attribute | Congruent Polygons | Similar Polygons |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Shape** | Identical | Identical |
| **Size** | Identical | Can be different (scaled) |
| **Corresponding Angles** | Congruent ($$\angle A \cong \angle P$$) | Congruent ($$\angle A \cong \angle P$$) |
| **Corresponding Sides** | Equal ($$AB = PQ$$) | Proportional ($$\frac{AB}{PQ} = k$$) |
| **Scale Factor ($$k$$)** | $$k = 1$$ | $$k > 0$$ (any positive constant) |

cards.title: 5.2 Similar Triangles and the Basic Proportionality Theorem
body: 5.2 Similar Triangles and the Basic Proportionality Theorem

**Definition:** **Similar Triangles** are triangles with congruent corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides. **The Basic Proportionality Theorem (BPT)** states that if a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle intersecting the other two sides in distinct points, then the other two sides are divided in the same ratio.

### Deep Dive
Triangles occupy a unique place in study of similarity. Unlike general polygons, we do not need to verify both angle congruence and side proportionality to prove that two triangles are similar. Because of the geometric constraints of three-sided figures, if one condition is met, the other is automatically satisfied. cards.title: Similarity and the Geometry of Shape
body: In engineering and construction, the Basic Proportionality Theorem is used to design stable structural frameworks, such as roof trusses and bridge supports. These structures use parallel beams to distribute loads evenly. The theorem allows designers to calculate the exact lengths of these support beams, ensuring structural safety.

Analyzing similar triangles also helps us understand coordinate geometry and trigonometry. The concept of **slope** along a straight line is constant because any two points on the line form similar slope triangles. This constant ratio of vertical rise to horizontal run is the geometric foundation of linear equations.

cards.problem: If the ratio of the perimeters of two similar polygons is $$3:4$$, what is the ratio of their corresponding side lengths?

steps.text: **Step 1: Apply the Perimeter Scale Factor relationship**

The perimeter of a polygon is a one-dimensional linear boundary measurement. Therefore, the ratio of the perimeters of similar polygons is exactly equal to the ratio of their corresponding side lengths (scale factor $$k$$).
Since the ratio of perimeters is $$3:4$$, the ratio of corresponding side lengths is also $$3:4$$.

cards.title: Similarity and the Geometry of Shape
body: It is important to note that satisfying only one of these conditions is not enough to guarantee similarity for polygons with more than three sides. For example, a square and a rectangle both have four right angles (congruent corresponding angles), but they are not similar because their sides are not proportional. Conversely, a square and a rhombus have proportional sides (all sides equal), but they are not similar because their corresponding angles are not equal. This shows that both angle congruence and side proportionality are required to establish similarity in general polygons.

cards.title: Similarity and the Geometry of Shape
body: > **💡 Did You Know?**: The concept of similarity allows us to calculate the height of massive structures using simple shadows. Around 600 BCE, the Greek philosopher Thales of Miletus calculated the height of the Great Pyramid of Giza by measuring its shadow at the exact time of day when his own shadow was equal to his height.

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: When setting up proportions for similar figures, always write the corresponding side lengths in the same order (e.g., $$\frac{\text{small shape}}{\text{large shape}} = \frac{\text{small shape}}{\text{large shape}}$$) to avoid inversion errors.

cards.title: Similarity and the Geometry of Shape
body: **SSS (Side-Side-Side) Similarity Theorems**.

The **AA Similarity Theorem** is the most commonly used. It states that if two angles of one triangle are congruent to two angles of another triangle, then the triangles are similar. This is because the sum of the angles in any triangle is always $$180^\circ$$, meaning the third pair of angles must also be congruent. The **SSS Similarity Theorem** states that if the corresponding sides of two triangles are proportional, then the triangles are similar. The **SAS Similarity Theorem** states that if an angle of one triangle is congruent to an angle of another triangle, and the sides including those angles are proportional, then the triangles are similar.

cards.title: Similarity and the Geometry of Shape
body:
| Theorem Name | Minimum Criteria | Geometric Conclusion |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **AA Similarity** | Two pairs of congruent corresponding angles. | $$\Delta ABC \sim \Delta DEF$$ |
| **SAS Similarity** | One pair of congruent angles, and the adjacent sides are proportional. | $$\Delta ABC \sim \Delta DEF$$ |
| **SSS Similarity** | All three pairs of corresponding sides are proportional. | $$\Delta ABC \sim \Delta DEF$$ |
| **Basic Proportionality (BPT)**| A line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle. | Divides the other two sides in the same ratio: $$\frac{AD}{DB} = \frac{AE}{EC}$$ |

> **💡 Did You Know?**: The Basic Proportionality Theorem is also known as Thales' Theorem, named after the ancient Greek mathematician Thales. It is widely considered the oldest formal mathematical proof in history.
